title: Read and write numbers from thousandths to billions, naming each place

lesson.title: Big Numbers, Little Numbers: Naming Every Place

steps.say: You already know how to read numbers up to one million, and how to read decimals all the way to thousandths. Today we stretch that same idea in both directions, so you can read a number as big as billions and as small as thousandths, and name every place along the way.

visual.caption: One million two hundred fifty thousand — you can already read this one

steps.say: Here is the secret: digits travel in families of three. Starting from the decimal point and moving left, the families are ones, then thousands, then millions, then billions. That is why we leave a little space between them. One billion is a one followed by nine zeros, which is a thousand millions.

visual.caption: One billion — a one with nine zeros after it

steps.say: Let us read a real one. Imagine a British Columbia bridge project costing three billion, four hundred five million dollars. Split the digits into families of three: three, then four zero five, then zero zero zero, then zero zero zero. Read each family, then say its family name. Three billion, four hundred five million. You do not say the empty thousands or ones families, because they are all zeros.

Now the tiny side. To the right of the decimal point the places are tenths, hundredths, and thousandths. If a hummingbird feather weighs zero point four zero six grams, the four sits in the tenths place, the zero sits in the hundredths place, and the six sits in the thousandths place. We read the whole group by its last place: four hundred six thousandths.

Here are two traps to dodge. Trap one: dropping a zero. Four thousand five is written four, zero, zero, five. Those two zeros are not nothing — they are holding the hundreds and tens seats. If you write four zero five instead, you have written four hundred five, a much smaller number. Trap two: mixing up families. One followed by six zeros is one million, but one followed by nine zeros is one billion — a thousand times bigger. Always count the families of three, not just the zeros.

visual.caption: The zeros are seat holders: 4 thousands, 0 hundreds, 0 tens, 5 ones

steps.say: So remember: chop the number into families of three going left, read each family and name it, and on the right side name the last decimal place. Every zero is a seat holder, so never let one sneak away.

lesson.answer: Read digits in families of three — ones, thousands, millions, billions — and every zero is holding a seat, so never drop it.

practice.question: A news story says a British Columbia hydro project cost two billion, forty million dollars. Write that amount in digits (you can draw your own place value chart to help). Then say which place the digit four is sitting in. Next, write four and six thousandths of a metre in digits.
practice.answer: Two billion, forty million dollars is 2 040 000 000. The four is in the ten millions place. Four and six thousandths of a metre is 4.006 metres — the two zeros hold the tenths and hundredths seats.
